blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Chapter 4 (Work, Energy and Power), arranged by the chapter's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each answer is a short model answer; small numericals show the working, and a comparison is answered as a table.
4.1 Work done by a constant force

blocks.prompt: 1 Define work done by a constant force. Write its formula when the force is along the displacement.
blocks.explanation: When a constant force F displaces an object through d in the direction of the force, work is the product of the magnitude of the force and the magnitude of the displacement: W = Fd. Work involves two things, force and displacement.

book_ref.quote: work W is defined as the product of the magnitude of the force F and magnitude of the displacement d

blocks.prompt: 2 A person pushing a wall gets tired, yet no work is done on the wall. Explain.
blocks.explanation: W = Fd. The wall does not move, so its displacement d = 0. If displacement is zero, no work is done even if a large force is applied; the muscles get tired but the work done on the wall is zero.

book_ref.quote: pushing on a wall may tire your muscles, but work done is zero

blocks.prompt: 3 Write the formula for work when the force F makes an angle θ with the displacement d. Show that work is a scalar.
blocks.explanation: Only the component of force along the displacement, F cos θ, does work: W = (F cos θ)d = Fd cos θ. In vector form W = F⃗·d⃗; the scalar (dot) product of two vectors is a scalar, so work is a scalar quantity.

book_ref.quote: If the force F makes an angle θ with the displacement d

blocks.prompt: 4 Define the joule.
blocks.explanation: The joule is the SI unit of work: 1 J = 1 N m. One joule of work is done when a force of 1 N moves a body through 1 m in the direction of the force (from W = Fd).

book_ref.quote: SI unit of work is N m known as joule (J).

blocks.prompt: 5 Under what conditions is the work done by a force positive, zero and negative?
blocks.explanation: From W = Fd cos θ: if θ < 90°, work is positive; if θ = 90°, cos θ = 0 and no work is done; if θ > 90°, cos θ is negative and the work done is negative.

book_ref.quote: If θ = 90°, no work is done.

blocks.prompt: 6 Differentiate between positive work and negative work.
blocks.explanation: Positive work: θ < 90°; negative work: θ > 90°.

book_ref.quote: If θ > 90°, the work done is said to be negative.

rows: Angle θ between force and displacement is less than 90°.
Angle θ between force and displacement is greater than 90°.
cos θ is positive, so W = Fd cos θ is positive.
cos θ is negative, so W = Fd cos θ is negative.
Example: gravity on a falling body.
Example: friction on a sliding body (θ = 180°).

blocks.prompt: 7 How can the work done by a constant force be found from a force-displacement graph?
blocks.explanation: Displacement is plotted on the x-axis and force on the y-axis. A constant force gives a horizontal straight line, and the rectangle under it has area F × d = Fd, the work done. So the area under the force-displacement graph represents the work done.

book_ref.quote: Hence, the area under a force-displacement curve can be taken as to represent the work done by the constant force.

blocks.prompt: 8 A force of 60 N pulls a box 4 m along the floor at 60° to the displacement. Find the work done.

book_ref.quote: the work done is equal to the product of the component of force along the direction of the displacement

blocks.prompt: 9 A frictional force of 12 N acts on a block as it slides 5 m. Find the work done by friction and state its sign.
blocks.explanation:
Friction acts opposite to the motion, θ = 180°.
W = Fd cos 180° = 12 × 5 × (−1) = −60 J
The work is negative because θ > 90°.

book_ref.quote: From the definition of work, we find that:

blocks.text: 4.2 Work done by a variable force

blocks.prompt: 10 What is a variable force? Give two examples from the chapter.
blocks.explanation: A variable force is one that does not remain constant while doing work. Examples: (i) the force of gravity on a rocket moving away from the Earth, which varies as the inverse square of the distance from the Earth's centre; (ii) the force exerted by a spring, which increases with the amount of stretch.

book_ref.quote: In many cases the force does not remain constant during the process of doing work.

blocks.prompt: 11 How is the work done by a variable force found graphically?
blocks.explanation: The displacement is divided into small intervals Δd in which the force is nearly constant; the work in each is the area of a rectangle Fᵢ cos θᵢ Δdᵢ. Adding them and letting Δd → 0 gives the area under the F cos θ versus d curve between P and Q, which is the work done.

book_ref.quote: Thus, the work done by a variable force in moving a particle between two points is equal to the area under the F cos θ verses d curve

blocks.prompt: 12 Why does the sum of rectangles give a more exact value of work when Δd is made smaller?
blocks.explanation: In each interval the force is only approximately constant. Smaller Δd means the force changes less within each interval, so the rectangles fit the curve better. When each Δd approaches zero, the sum becomes exact (Eq. 4.5).

book_ref.quote: If we let each Δd to approach zero, then we obtain an exact result for the work done

blocks.prompt: 13 A force is 6 N from d = 0 to d = 5 m and then decreases uniformly to zero at d = 8 m. Find the work done from d = 0 to d = 8 m.
blocks.explanation:
Work = area under the curve
Rectangle: 6 N × 5 m = 30 J
Triangle: ½ × 3 m × 6 N = 9 J
Total work = 30 + 9 = 39 J

book_ref.quote: This area is equal to the area of the rectangular section from d = 0 to d = 4 m

blocks.prompt: 14 What is the gravitational field? When is the work done by gravity positive and when negative?
blocks.explanation: The space around the Earth in which its gravitational force acts on a body is the gravitational field. If the displacement is in the direction of the gravitational force (falling), the work is positive; if it is against the gravitational force (rising), the work is negative.

book_ref.quote: The space around the Earth in which its gravitational force acts on a body is called the gravitational field.

blocks.prompt: 15 Define a conservative force and give three examples.
blocks.explanation: A force is conservative if the work done by it in moving an object between two points is independent of the path followed, or the work done in a closed path is zero. Examples: gravitational force, electrostatic force, elastic spring force.

book_ref.quote: If the work done by a force in moving an object between two points is independent of the path followed

blocks.prompt: 16 When a curved path in the gravitational field is broken into small steps, why is no work done by gravity along the horizontal steps?
blocks.explanation: Along a horizontal step, the weight mg is perpendicular to the displacement (θ = 90°, cos 90° = 0), so W = 0. Work by gravity is done only along the vertical steps, and these add up to h, giving −mgh for a rise h.

book_ref.quote: There is no work done along the horizontal steps, because mg is perpendicular to the displacement for these steps.

blocks.prompt: 17 Show that the work done by gravity along a closed path such as ACBA is zero.
blocks.explanation: From A to B (rise h) by path ACB: W = −mgh + 0 = −mgh. From B back to A (fall h): the displacement is along mg, W = +mgh. Total = −mgh + mgh = 0. Hence gravity is a conservative force.

book_ref.quote: Can you prove that the work done, along a closed path, such as ACBA or ADBA (Fig. 4.9), by the gravitational force is zero?

blocks.prompt: 18 A 3 kg box is raised 4 m, once by a vertical lift and once along a long ramp. Find the work done by gravity in each case.
blocks.explanation:
Work by gravity is independent of the path.
W = −mgh = −3 × 9.8 × 4 = −117.6 J ≈ −118 J in both cases.

book_ref.quote: Work done by gravitational force is independent of the path followed.

blocks.prompt: 19 Define a non-conservative force and give three examples.
blocks.explanation: A force is non-conservative if the work done by it in moving an object between two points, or in a closed path, depends on the path of motion. Examples: kinetic friction, air resistance, tension in a string (also normal force, propulsion force of a rocket).

book_ref.quote: A force is non-conservative if the work done by it in moving an object between two points or in a closed path depends on the path of motion.

blocks.prompt: 20 A crate is dragged from P to Q against a friction of 6 N along a straight 5 m path and along a curved 9 m path. Find the work done by friction in each case. What does the result show?
blocks.explanation:
Friction does negative work = f × path length.
Straight: −6 × 5 = −30 J; curved: −6 × 9 = −54 J
The work depends on the path, so friction is non-conservative.

book_ref.quote: Thus, greater amount of work is done over a longer path between any two points.

blocks.prompt: 21 Differentiate between conservative and non-conservative forces.
blocks.explanation: Conservative: work independent of path; non-conservative: work depends on path.

book_ref.quote: the force is called a conservative force

rows: Work done between two points is independent of the path followed.
Work done between two points depends on the path of motion.
Work done in a closed path is zero.
Work done in a closed path is not zero.
Examples: gravitational, electrostatic, elastic spring force.
Examples: kinetic friction, air resistance, tension, normal force, rocket propulsion.

blocks.prompt: 22 Define power and average power. Is power a scalar or a vector?
blocks.explanation: Power is the measure of the rate at which work is being done. If work ΔW is done in time Δt, average power P_av = ΔW/Δt. Power is a scalar, since work and time are both scalars.

book_ref.quote: Power is the measure of the rate at which work is being done.

blocks.prompt: 23 Define instantaneous power.
blocks.explanation: If work is expressed as a function of time, the instantaneous power at any instant is the limit of ΔW/Δt as Δt approaches zero: P = lim (Δt → 0) ΔW/Δt, where ΔW is the work done in the short time interval Δt.

book_ref.quote: If work is expressed as a function of time, the instantaneous power P at any instant is defined as:

blocks.prompt: 24 Show that power is the dot product of force and velocity.
blocks.explanation: P = ΔW/Δt and ΔW = F⃗·Δd⃗, so P = F⃗·Δd⃗/Δt = F⃗·(Δd⃗/Δt). Since Δd⃗/Δt = v⃗, P = F⃗·v⃗ (Eq. 4.8).

book_ref.quote: where ΔW is the work done in short interval of time Δt.

blocks.prompt: 25 Define the watt. Express it in base units.
blocks.explanation: The watt is the SI unit of power: one joule of work done in one second, 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹. In base units, 1 W = 1 kg m² s⁻² / s = 1 kg m² s⁻³.

book_ref.quote: The SI unit of power is watt, defined as one joule of work done in one second.

blocks.prompt: 26 Define kilowatt-hour and show that 1 kW h = 3.6 MJ.
blocks.explanation:
One kilowatt-hour is the work done in one hour by an agency whose power is one kilowatt; it is the commercial unit of electrical energy.
1 kW h = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J = 3.6 MJ

book_ref.quote: One kilowatt- hour is the work done in one hour by an agency whose power is one kilowatt.

blocks.prompt: 27 Why is power more useful than work alone in practical applications?
blocks.explanation: The definition of work does not tell whether the work is done in one second or in one hour. In practice we need to know how fast work is done, i.e. the rate of doing work, which is power.

book_ref.quote: In the definition of work, it is not clear, whether the same amount of work is done in one second or in one hour.

blocks.prompt: 28 Differentiate between work and power.
blocks.explanation: Work is force × displacement; power is the rate of doing work.

book_ref.quote: If work ΔW is done in a time interval Δt

rows: Product of force and displacement: W = F⃗·d⃗.
Rate of doing work: P = ΔW/Δt = F⃗·v⃗.
Does not tell how fast the work is done.
Tells how fast the work is done.
SI unit: joule (J).
SI unit: watt (W) = J s⁻¹.

blocks.prompt: 29 A 65 kg student climbs stairs of vertical height 5.0 m in 6.5 s. Find the student's power output.

book_ref.quote: The vertical height of the stairs is 4.5 m. Calculate his power output in watts.

blocks.prompt: 30 A boat engine exerts a forward force of 800 N while the boat moves at a steady 15 m s⁻¹ in the same direction. Find the power of the engine.

book_ref.quote: where ΔW is the work done in short interval of time Δt.

blocks.prompt: 31 A 1.5 kW iron is used for 4 hours. Find the energy used in kW h and in joules.

book_ref.quote: However, a commercial unit of electrical energy is kilowatt-hour.

blocks.prompt: 32 Define energy. Name its two basic forms.
blocks.explanation: Energy of a body is its capacity to do work. Its two basic forms are kinetic energy and potential energy; both are kinds of mechanical energy.

book_ref.quote: Energy of a body is its capacity to do work.

blocks.prompt: 33 Differentiate between kinetic energy and potential energy.
blocks.explanation: Kinetic energy is due to motion; potential energy is due to position or constrained state.

book_ref.quote: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its motion

rows: Energy possessed by a body due to its motion.
Energy possessed by a body due to its changed position or constrained state.
K.E. = ½mv².
Near the Earth P.E. = mgh; absolute P.E. U = −GMm/r.
Example: a moving car.
Example: a compressed spring (elastic P.E.).

blocks.prompt: 34 Why is the kinetic energy of a car taken equal to fd, where f is friction and d the stopping distance?
blocks.explanation: When the engine is switched off, the moving car still covers a distance d against friction f before stopping, doing work fd. This work is done due to its motion. The ability of a body to do work due to its motion is its kinetic energy, so K.E. = fd.

book_ref.quote: As long as it is moving, it is doing work against the force of friction of the road.

blocks.prompt: 35 Why is the unit of kinetic energy the same as that of work?
blocks.explanation: Kinetic energy is equal to the work which the body is capable of doing because of its motion. So its unit must be that of work, the joule (J).

book_ref.quote: Since, kinetic energy is equal to work which the body is capable of doing

blocks.prompt: 36 A cricket ball of mass 0.15 kg moves at 20 m s⁻¹. Find its kinetic energy.

book_ref.quote: Let us derive a formula for the kinetic energy of a moving body.

blocks.prompt: 37 How does the kinetic energy of a body change if its speed is made three times?
blocks.explanation: K.E. = ½mv², so K.E. ∝ v². If v becomes 3v, K.E. becomes ½m(3v)² = 9 × ½mv², i.e. nine times.

book_ref.quote: The ability of a body to do work due to its motion is its kinetic energy.

blocks.prompt: 38 A car of weight 11760 N moving at 12 m s⁻¹ is stopped by its brakes in 36 m. Find the average force of friction.

book_ref.quote: Determine the average force of friction acting on it.

blocks.prompt: 39 What is elastic potential energy? Give an example.
blocks.explanation: Potential energy possessed by a body because of its constrained (compressed or stretched) state is elastic potential energy. Example: the energy stored in a compressed spring.

book_ref.quote: The energy stored in a compressed spring is the potential energy possessed by the spring due to its compressed or stretched state.

blocks.prompt: 40 Define absolute gravitational potential energy and write its formula.
blocks.explanation: The absolute gravitational potential energy of an object at a position is the work done by the gravitational force in displacing it from that position to infinity, where the force of gravity becomes zero. U = −GMm/r, where r is the distance from the Earth's centre.

book_ref.quote: The absolute gravitational potential energy of an object at a certain position is the work done by the gravitational force

blocks.prompt: 41 Why can P.E. = mgh not be used when a body is moved through a large distance in space?
blocks.explanation: mgh is true only near the Earth's surface where the gravitational force is nearly constant. Over a large distance the gravitational force does not remain constant; it varies inversely as the square of the distance, so the work must be found by adding small steps.

book_ref.quote: But if the body is displaced through a large distance in space

blocks.prompt: 42 Why is the absolute gravitational potential energy negative?
blocks.explanation: U = −GMm/r. The P.E. is zero at infinity, and work must be done on the body to take it there against gravity, so below infinity it is less than zero. The negative sign shows that the Earth's gravitational field for mass m is attractive.

book_ref.quote: The negative sign shows that the Earth's gravitational field for mass m is attractive.

blocks.prompt: 43 How does the absolute P.E. of a body change when it is raised above the Earth's surface?
blocks.explanation: U = −GMm/r. When r increases, U becomes less negative, i.e. U increases. So raising a body increases its P.E.; at infinity it becomes zero, after work GMm/R has been done on it from the surface.

book_ref.quote: It means when we raise a body above the surface of the Earth, its P.E. increases.

blocks.prompt: 44 In the derivation of absolute P.E., show that r² = r₁r₂ for a small step.
blocks.explanation: r = r₁ + Δr/2, so r² = r₁² + r₁Δr + (Δr/2)². As (Δr)² << r₁², it is neglected: r² = r₁² + r₁Δr. Putting Δr = r₂ − r₁: r² = r₁² + r₁(r₂ − r₁) = r₁r₂.

book_ref.quote: As (Δr)² << r₁², so (Δr)² can be neglected as compared to r₁².

blocks.prompt: 45 A 2 kg bag is lifted from the floor to a shelf 6 m high. Find the gain in its potential energy.
blocks.explanation:
Near the Earth's surface, P.E. = mgh
= 2 × 9.8 × 6 = 117.6 J ≈ 118 J

book_ref.quote: The relation for the calculation of the work done by the gravitational force or potential energy is mgh

blocks.prompt: 46 Differentiate between gravitational P.E. near the Earth (mgh) and absolute gravitational P.E.
blocks.explanation: mgh holds near the surface; −GMm/r holds at any distance and is zero at infinity.

book_ref.quote: where its potential energy with respect to Earth is zero

rows: True only near the Earth's surface, where gravity is nearly constant.
True at any distance r from the Earth's centre; gravity varies as 1/r².
Measured from a chosen level such as the ground.
Measured with zero P.E. at infinity.
Positive above the chosen level.
Always negative; becomes less negative as r increases.

blocks.prompt: 47 Define escape velocity. What is its approximate value for the Earth?
blocks.explanation: The initial velocity with which an object goes out of the Earth's gravitational field is the escape velocity. For the Earth it is approximately 11 km s⁻¹ (11.2 km s⁻¹ in the table).

book_ref.quote: The initial velocity of an object with which it goes out of the Earth's gravitational field, is known as escape velocity.

blocks.prompt: 48 Why does an object thrown upward come back, and when will it not come back?
blocks.explanation: It comes back because the force of gravity acts downward on it. With a greater initial velocity it rises higher; if the initial velocity is increased to the escape velocity, it will not return and escapes out of the influence of gravity.

book_ref.quote: This is due to the force of gravity acting downward.

blocks.prompt: 49 Does the escape velocity depend on the mass of the projected body? Explain.
blocks.explanation: No. At escape, ½mv_esc² = GMm/R; the mass m of the body cancels, giving v_esc = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR), which depends only on the mass M (or g) and radius R of the Earth.

book_ref.quote: The body will escape out of the gravitational field if the initial K.E. of the body is equal to increase in P.E.

blocks.prompt: 50 Why do the Moon and Jupiter have very different escape speeds?
blocks.explanation: v_esc = √(2GM/R) depends on the mass and radius of the heavenly body. The Moon's mass is small, giving only 2.4 km s⁻¹, while massive Jupiter has 61 km s⁻¹ (table).

book_ref.quote: For Your Information: Some Escape speeds (km s⁻¹)

blocks.prompt: 51 A planet has g = 3.7 m s⁻² at its surface and radius 3.4 × 10⁶ m. Find the escape velocity from it.

book_ref.quote: where M and R are the mass and radius of the Earth respectively.

blocks.prompt: 52 State the work-energy theorem and write it as an equation.
blocks.explanation:
The change in kinetic energy of an object is equal to the work done on it by a net force:
W = Fd = (K.E.)f − (K.E.)i = ½mvf² − ½mvi²

book_ref.quote: The change in kinetic energy of an object is equal to the work done on it by a net force.

blocks.prompt: 53 Is the work-energy theorem valid when the force is opposite to the motion, or when the force varies? Explain.
blocks.explanation: Yes. It applies for any direction of the force relative to the displacement: when an object with K.E. pushes or pulls another object, the work is negative and its K.E. decreases. It also remains valid if the force varies from point to point.

book_ref.quote: For instance, an object with kinetic energy can perform work if it is allowed to push or pull on another object.

blocks.prompt: 54 A 3 kg trolley speeds up from 4 m s⁻¹ to 10 m s⁻¹. Find the work done on it by the net force.

book_ref.quote: Whenever work is done on a body, it increases its energy.

blocks.prompt: 55 A net force of 20 N acts on a 4 kg body at rest through 8 m. Find its final speed.
blocks.explanation:
Fd = ½mvf² − 0: 20 × 8 = ½ × 4 × vf²
160 = 2vf², vf² = 80, vf = 8.9 m s⁻¹

book_ref.quote: This expression is the work-energy theorem. It states that:

blocks.prompt: 56 For a body sliding down a slope with friction, which force does work and which does not?
blocks.explanation: The normal force F_N is balanced by mg cos θ and is perpendicular to the motion, so it does no work. The net force along the slope, F = mg sin θ − f, does work Fd, which equals the change in K.E.

book_ref.quote: The normal force F_N is balanced by the component of weight (mg cos 24°) perpendicular to the slope.

blocks.text: 4.8 Interconversion of potential energy and kinetic energy

blocks.prompt: 57 Show that the total energy of a freely falling body remains mgh at a point where it has fallen a distance x.
blocks.explanation:
At B, P.E. = mg(h − x). From vB² = 2gx, K.E. = ½m(2gx) = mgx.
Total energy = mg(h − x) + mgx = mgh, the same as at the start (air friction ignored).

book_ref.quote: Total energy at position B = P.E. + K.E.

blocks.prompt: 58 Show that just before a falling body strikes the ground, its K.E. equals its original P.E.
blocks.explanation:
At C, P.E. = 0 and vC² = 2gh (vi = 0).
K.E. = ½mvC² = ½m × 2gh = mgh, the original P.E. at A.

book_ref.quote: Thus, at point C, kinetic energy is equal to the original value of the potential energy of the body.

blocks.prompt: 59 Write the relation between loss in P.E. and gain in K.E. for a falling body. When is it true?
blocks.explanation: Loss in P.E. = Gain in K.E.: mg(h₁ − h₂) = ½m(v₂² − v₁²), where v₁ and v₂ are the velocities at heights h₁ and h₂. It is true only when frictional force is not considered.

book_ref.quote: This result is true only when frictional force is not considered.

blocks.prompt: 60 How is the energy equation of a falling body changed when air friction f is present?
blocks.explanation:
Part of the P.E. is used in doing work fh against friction; only the remaining mgh − fh becomes K.E.:
mgh = ½mv² + fh, i.e. Loss in P.E. = Gain in K.E. + Work done against friction.

book_ref.quote: then a part of P.E. is used in doing work against friction equal to f h

blocks.prompt: 61 A 0.5 kg stone is dropped from a height of 12 m. Find its speed just before it hits the ground (ignore air friction).
blocks.explanation:
Loss in P.E. = Gain in K.E.: mgh = ½mv²
v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.8 × 12) = √235.2 = 15.3 m s⁻¹

book_ref.quote: Velocity v_B, at position B, can be calculated from the relation,

blocks.prompt: 62 A 2 kg body falls from a height of 25 m and strikes the ground at 20 m s⁻¹. Find the average air friction on it.

book_ref.quote: If it strikes the ground with a velocity of 16 m s⁻¹, calculate the average frictional force of the air.

blocks.prompt: 63 A body is dropped from a height of 20 m. At what height above the ground are its K.E. and P.E. equal (no air friction)?
blocks.explanation:
Total energy = mgh stays constant. When K.E. = P.E., each is ½mgh.
mg × (height) = ½mg × 20, so height = 10 m above the ground (it has fallen x = 10 m).

book_ref.quote: We release the body and as it falls, we can examine how kinetic and potential energies associated with it interchange.

blocks.prompt: 64 A car with its engine off coasts up a rough slope. Write the energy relation for its motion.
blocks.explanation:
Its K.E. is partly converted into P.E. and partly used up in doing work against friction:
Loss of K.E. = Gain in P.E. + Work done against friction
½m(vi² − vf²) = mgh + fd

book_ref.quote: The kinetic energy possessed by the car at point P will partly be converted into P.E. and partly used up in doing work against friction
